#7564. Gamers Love Ad Blockers. So This Site Found Another Way To Show Them Ads

Ad blocking doesn’t just prevent publishers from earning revenue; it also creates blind spots in their audience analytics that can affect everything from monetization strategy to editorial coverage.

Gamers are very likely to use ad blockers, which has led to significant challenges for WiseGuyGaming, a video game-focused publication that launched last year.

Its co-founder and CEO, Mike Smith, launched the publication with his son Mikhail following previous stints handling audience data and monetization for HBO, Forbes and Hearst. After two-plus decades working at established media brands, he wanted to start his own, he told AdExchanger.

However, the elder Smith quickly realized that the audience he most wanted to reach – technologically sophisticated gamers – are disproportionately likely to use the most advanced ad blockers on the market. Those ad blockers made this audience largely invisible to existing analytics solutions, in addition to being unreachable with banner and video ads.

As a result, WiseGuyGaming found that about 18% of its audience used ad-blocking tech. Now it’s strategizing how to reach that audience in ways that can’t be blocked as easily as a web banner.

In addition to the Google Analytics tools widely used by publishers, WiseGuyGaming also relies on another popular third-party audience analytics and bot filtration tool, FouAnalytics, to measure its audience.

It’s especially important for publishers to use multiple analytics solutions these days, Marti said, because an explosion in bot-crawling activity to support generative and agentic AI has made it harder to separate human site visitors from bots.

Plus, Marti said, there are now more services like Bright Data that turn consumer devices like cellphones and TVs into residential proxies for AI scraping and other bot activity.

Basically, if an app installed on a person’s TV partners with Bright Data, that person can opt in to allow their IP address to be used to mask bot behavior. In exchange, they get an ad-free experience when using the app or some other incentive.

These proxy services make it harder for publishers to weed out bots using traditional methods like blocking IP addresses associated with previous bot activity, Marti said. Proxy services can make a bot appear to be using a residential IP address, rather than one tied to a data center.

However, there are nuances in how bot crawlers work when they load a publisher page that can be exploited to detect them, Marti said.

For instance, he said, many crawlers are configured to scrape a website’s data before any third-party scripts – including ad tech and bot-blocking tech – are able to execute on the page.

“The crawling company has been told, ‘Go to this page and [extract] the content of the big table on that page as JSON,’” Marti said. “The crawler is smart enough to know that all the social widgets on the page, all the random third-party JavaScript, ads, analytics – it doesn’t need that for the mission it’s on.” The crawler’s headless browser often doesn’t even bother sending the network requests required for the third-party scripts to run, he said.

But, as it turns out, Marti added, ad blockers likewise prevent the browser from sending network requests to ping third-party scripts, including ad tech and analytics. Which means publishers can use more advanced bot-detection strategies to also reveal when a human site visitor is using an ad blocker.

When a user with an ad blocker arrives on the page, the ad blocker references lists of known third-party ad servers and domains associated with ad tech, then prevents network requests from pinging those servers and domains.

Marti and Smith’s solution was to set up two versions of FouAnalytics on the WiseGuyGaming site.

But the other version used a “proxy pass” – or a first-party URL – to obscure the third-party script, he said. “It’s on wiseguygaming.com, so it’s not going to show up on any of the filter lists. But it is proxied through to the same FouAnalytics server as the third-party script, so we’ve got the exact same script being served onto the page twice.”

WiseGuyGaming could then compare data between its two different FouAnalytics dashboards to see which users were blocking the FouAnalytics third-party script, but not blocking FouAnalytics when it was using the proxy pass.

And since both Google Analytics and FouAnalytics had already prefiltered out likely bots, WiseGuyGaming could conclude with reasonable certainty that the remaining 18% still blocking FouAnalytics as a third-party script were probably either invalid traffic that evaded the bot filter or humans using an ad blocker.

Once WiseGuyGaming nailed down that roughly 18% figure for its ad-blocking audience, it then had to come up with a new way to reach those users, since banner ads wouldn’t cut it.

WiseGuyGaming’s immediate solution was to produce more sponsored and native content, which ad blockers are not configured to recognize, Smith said.

Meanwhile, the site’s editorial team was able to analyze the ad-blocking audience’s traffic patterns to understand what content was resonating with them, Smith said. Which is helping the editors to publish more content that can bring in that highly technical audience the Smiths want to reach.

The solution did have one flaw, Marti noted. It required them to look at two different FouAnalytics dashboards in two different browser tabs to compare the ad-blocking and non-ad-blocking audiences.

But that’s a minor concern, since the solution has transformed WiseGuyGaming’s editorial and monetization strategies, Smith said.

“We set out first to get a very pure count of our audience,” he said. “We are now going to launch a paid subscription service and use email and push [notification] technology to reach the roughly 18% that we found.”

#7562. Ads Drive Consumer Demand. The Shelf Captures It

Imagine you’re shopping for laundry detergent. You click to buy your preferred brand, but when your order is fulfilled, the product is out of stock. What do you do?

Recent DoorDash data shows that shoppers in this scenario buy a competing brand nearly 12% of the time, while more than 40% of the time they request a refund instead. In either case, the preferred brand just lost an easy opportunity to convert on strong demand.

This isn’t a niche problem. Inventory distortion from out-of-stocks and overstocks costs the retail industry an estimated $1.7 trillion each year, according to IHL Group. That makes capturing that demand a huge growth opportunity for brands.

The challenge here is that most commerce media platforms are great at measuring advertising performance but don’t fully understand the conditions under which advertising is trying to convert. That missing context is becoming increasingly consequential as brands invest more heavily in commerce media.

Commerce media’s greatest strength is proximity to the transaction. Advertisers can connect media exposure to purchases and measure impact against verified sales.

But many other factors can derail conversion. A product might be missing from the retailer’s digital assortment, or the listing might lack a title, image or product detail to give the shopper confidence. In each case, the brand doesn’t have a full view of the lost opportunity.

Conventional advertising metrics can tell us what happened (click/no click, sale/no sale, etc.), but often lack the context to explain why or why not, as the case may be. And if marketers don’t understand why something happened, it’s easy to optimize for the wrong variable.

When a campaign delivers strong engagement but disappointing sales or category share, the natural response is to adjust the media strategy by changing the targeting or creative or shifting spending toward other products or retailers. But what if the campaign was reaching the right consumers and generating genuine purchase intent only to encounter one of the availability problems discussed above?

In that case, shifting budget away from the “underperforming” product or retailer actually means walking away from demonstrated consumer demand.

The same applies to substitution behavior. When shoppers can’t get their preferred product, do they choose another product within the brand’s portfolio, switch to a competitor or abandon the purchase altogether?

Each of those actions merits a distinct strategic response. A product that consistently loses shoppers to competitors during stockouts might warrant greater attention from sales and supply-chain teams. A product with strong demand but poor digital visibility might need better catalog execution to maximize advertising outcomes.

The takeaway is that advertising amplifies demand and content drives conversion – but growth is delivered on the shelf. And without visibility into that full order journey, it’s easy to pour money into fixing a problem that doesn’t exist.

These gaps in contextual understanding stem from a familiar problem in ad tech: fragmented workflows and siloed data. Marketing teams manage campaign strategy, delivery and performance. Ecommerce oversees product listings and content. Sales and category teams manage retailer relationships and assortment. Supply-chain teams focus on inventory and availability.

Organizations haven’t connected the data in a way that helps them understand if and where demand hits a snag along the buying journey. For decades, point of sale and syndicated sales data has helped CPGs understand what sold in stores. But sales data alone rarely explains why a product didn’t sell. Was it out of stock? Was the shopper’s preferred item or size unavailable? Did they choose another product or switch to a competitor when at the shelf?

But even when brands have inventory data, they can’t always keep up with what shoppers encounter. Shelves change by the hour and any data source – whether it’s a brand’s, a retailer’s or a periodic audit – is just a snapshot.

Newer approaches are helping close that gap by connecting advertising data with real-world commerce signals. At DoorDash, for example, we’re evolving Ads Manager into Brand Center, bringing advertising performance together with on-shelf availability, assortment insights and consumer purchasing insights. By combining order data with in-store signals captured by Dashers, brands can see not only where sales are happening, but where demand may be going unfulfilled due to out-of-stocks and what shoppers choose instead when a product isn’t available.

This integrated visibility is helping different teams within an organization work from a shared understanding of what’s constraining growth so they can figure out who can actually do something about it.

Commerce media has rapidly become a core marketing channel because of how it’s made advertising more measurable and more optimizable. But to mature further, commerce media performance needs to be connected with the broader commercial context that determines whether demand becomes revenue.

That deeper contextual visibility brings a new set of questions that lead to critical insights, including, “Which products are generating demand that isn’t being fulfilled?” and “Where are availability or assortment gaps suppressing sales?”

Marketers don’t have to become inventory managers or supply-chain experts. But they should have enough visibility to recognize when a disappointing campaign result isn’t actually an advertising problem. Because a commerce media program with impressive advertising metrics isn’t worth much if it’s not driving real revenue.

Sometimes, the best way to improve advertising performance has nothing to do with the ad itself.

#7560. The poisoned public rights doctrine and Sun Valley Orchards

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

On Tuesday, Nov. 10, the court will hear argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC. This case concerns the H-2A visa program for temporary alien immigrant workers. The issue is whether the Department of Labor’s Article II administrative law judges have the authority to collect ruinous fines from employers who violate their employment contracts with such individuals.

In early August of this year, I signed an amicus brief supporting Sun Valley Orchards along with former Attorneys General Edwin Meese III and Michael Mukasey and law professor Gary Lawson, prepared and filed by our lawyer Amit Vora. We argued that the respondent was entitled not only to a Seventh Amendment civil jury but also to an Article III federal court.

After reading the government’s opening and reply briefs by Solicitor General D. John Sauer, I stand by our argument that a DOL administrative law judge may not deprive Sun Valley of property by imposing ruinous fines for violating a contract that bound it to follow certain labor laws in employing foreign immigrant H-2A workers. Rather, Sun Valley has a Seventh Amendment right to have its claims heard by a jury if it desires to do so.

The government is obviously correct that the government has a sovereign right to control immigration into the United States under the H-2A program. It does not follow from that, however, that the government can condition the admission of foreign workers under this program on Sun Valley’s surrendering its constitutional right to have employment disputes with those workers adjudicated by Article III courts with a Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial. Constitutional rights cannot be taken away without due process of law or in violation of, for example, the First, Fourth, or Seventh amendments. But that is exactly what the government is trying to do in this case.

By way of example, in 1987’s Nollan v. California Coastal Commission, the Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Antonin Scalia, held that the California Coastal Commission could not use its plenary power over zoning to condition a renovation construction permit on the Nolans ceding a public easement to walk along their valuable California coastal property, as doing so would violate the takings clause of the Fifth Amendment. Likewise, the government cannot impose unconstitutional conditions when using either its zoning power or its plenary power over immigration. Nor can the government use its commerce power or any of its other enumerated powers to violate one’s constitutional rights. The government can shut down the foreign immigrant H2A program. But it cannot use it as a cudgel to make Americans surrender their constitutional rights simply because the rights of immigrants are at stake.

Central to the government’s argument otherwise is the public-rights doctrine. This doctrine – properly understood – allows for privileges created by the government to be adjudicated by non-Article III judges, such as the privileges to receive social-security, disability, or welfare payments; the privilege to immigrate into the United States; or the privilege to receive tax rebates under the federal government’s partial waiver of sovereign immunity. With regard to such privileges, the Constitution’s guarantee of an Article III forum and the Seventh Amendment civil jury trial right are inapplicable because the receipt of these were not property rights recognized at common law, but privileges created by the government. The government argues that because immigration into the country is also a privilege, not a right, Sun Valley’s conduct related to this are not subject to Article III protections.

It is true that the public rights doctrine was profoundly altered (one could say poisoned), in the 1977 case of Atlas Roofing Co. v. Occupational Safety and Health Administration. In Atlas Roofing, Justice Byron White denied access to an Article III court and a Seventh Amendment civil jury trial to a party subject to an OSHA enforcement order. According to White, because such orders were based on “new statutory obligations,” they could be “committed exclusively to an administrative agency [for] deciding whether a violation has in fact occurred.” This was incorrect: while OSHA created new torts that can occur in the workplace, these were analogous to the kinds of tort actions that would have been heard at common law. Indeed, such torts are classic “Cases in Law,” which Article III gives sole jurisdiction over to life-tenured federal judges assisted by a civil jury if the plaintiffs choose one. Thus, Atlas Roofing Co. changed the law to say that the public-rights doctrine not only allowed Article II administrative law judges to deprive persons of privileges, but, for the first time, it also eliminated the guarantee of a Seventh Amendment jury trial when a person or entity was deprived of property rights by the government.

Fortunately, this dangerous precedent was limited by the more recent 2024 case of SEC v. Jarkesy. In Jarkesy, the Supreme Court held that when the SEC imposed civil penalties against a defendant for securities fraud, the Seventh Amendment entitled the defendant to a jury trial. This is because in 1787 a fraud case, like the employment contract case at issue in Sun Valley (or, for that matter, the property seized in Atlas Roofing), would have been “Case in Law” assigned to the sole jurisdiction of the Article III courts.

So the lesson of Jarkesy is this: While the vast majority of cases which ALJs decide only “privileges” and not “rights” only require an Article II hearing, when federal regulatory agencies impose ruinous fines on a corporation or person, those fines are deprivations of one’s right to property. And in depriving one of such property, it is not enough to have an administrative hearing: The case must be heard by an Article III court with the right to a Seventh Amendment civil-jury trial.

The public-rights doctrine then does not apply to enforcement orders that deprive a person of property by agencies such as OSHA in Atlas Roofing, the SEC in Jarkesy, or the DOL in Sun Valley. Nor does calling a case an immigration matter empower the government to take away the constitutional rights of Americans even if immigration into the United States is itself a privilege and not a right.

So let’s hope that the Supreme Court in Sun Valley rejects, as unconstitutional, the DOL’s attempt to funnel a private-rights dispute away from an Article III forum. And let’s further hope that the court clearly reframes the public-rights doctrine, as limited in Jarkesy, as a mere manifestation of the rights/privileges distinction – and continues to prevent the doctrine from taking the form that Justice White allowed for in Atlas Roofing: an ominous threat to Article III, the Seventh Amendment, and the due process clause.

Professor Steven Gow Calabresi is the Clayton J. & Henry R. Barber Professor of Law at Northwestern Pritzker School of Law.

Recommended Citation: Steven Gow Calabresi, The poisoned public rights doctrine and Sun Valley Orchards, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 6, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-poisoned-public-rights-doctrine-and-sun-valley-orchards/

#7557. AppLovin Is Back To Smashing Earnings, But Investors Are Slow To Buy

AppLovin is growing at a blistering pace, but Wall Street investors remain cautious about the business.

The mobile ad tech company earned just shy of $2.2 billion in Q3 this year, per the company’s earnings report after-hours on Wednesday. Of that, $1.44 billion fell straight to net income (which is to say, profit). That is an “industry-leading” profit margin of about 66%, said CFO Matthew Stumpf.

It’s the type of number ad tech companies haven’t seen since Rocket Fuel hit the market. Which, admittedly, isn’t such fantastic company, considering Rocket Fuel’s disastrous downfall. But that association – not with Rocket Fuel, but with third-party ad tech – is part of the challenge for AppLovin.

Co-Founder and CEO Adam Foroughi addressed the education and mind-shifting among media buyers (and, ahem, among its investors) that needs to happen for its consumer ad business to accelerate.

“People have to go, ‘This is a bigger ad tech company, that’s sort-of-independent ad tech without a first-party site, [and] bigger than anything we’ve ever seen before,’” Foroughi told investors.

There is a great deal of “headroom for growth,” as Foroughi put it multiple times throughout the call, when it comes to the consumer ad business. But filling that headroom is going to take a lot of time.

Right now, AppLovin’s consumer ads segment is growing fast – more than 100% year over year, Foroughi said, though revenue for that segment is not disclosed. That business was only formally launched out of beta last year, so the revenue is still relatively low. The business will compound over time, he said, as advertisers figure out the platform and run incrementality attribution studies to feel confident with the ROAS.

Foroughi pointed to the changes Apple is making to iOS and mobile web inventory as another reason for advertisers to get on board with AppLovin’s platform.

“A lot of what’s called, I guess, traditionally, ‘open web,’” Foroughi said, is actually just a cheap reach play. That mentality is not like AppLovin’s ad system, which tracks and values impressions through to the point of conversion, he said. A healthy platform with strong ROAS may very well see CPM increases, despite being antithetical to the cheap reach mindset. But the mobile gaming space is “much, much bigger” now, he added, and the web is becoming less trackable.

“We think a lot of those dollars will shift into the app space,” he said.

Then there’s AppLovin’s creative knowledge gap.

Advertisers in the consumer segment have mostly not purchased ads in mobile games before, nor are they familiar with the particulars of how AppLovin’s media platform works, according to Fouroughi.  Mobile game advertisers all use the platform already, and they have specific creative that, say, offers a mini-game or test gameplay to prompt a download. Ecommerce advertisers on social media can’t just port over their creatives.

For one thing, he said that social platforms are all about super-quick videos with a hook delivered in a second or two. But AppLovin’s gaming audience is watching a full-screen ad for 30-60 seconds. It practically never happens on a social feed.

“There’s a learning process here that has to happen so that the media buyers really understand the framework,” Foroughi said.

Eventually, agencies and advertisers will figure it out and approach AppLovin as an always-on platform with a standardized approach to creative.

“There will be playbooks for our platform,” he prophesied.

AppLovin laid out an ambitious marker on its earnings call.

“We believe this business can compound at roughly 30% annually over the long term,” Foroughi said of the ad tech business.

The current earnings report has ad revenue up by 55% and a profit margin that, as Foroughi put it, “is probably second to none.”

But 30% growth over the long term is bold, considering the multibillion-dollar scale of AppLovin’s ad business. And investors are still wary.

Some advertisers purportedly anticipate price hikes on AppLovin, since there are now gaming and consumer advertisers bidding for the same impressions, Stephen Ju of UBS Investment Bank noted.

Matthew Cost of Morgan Stanley wondered when the “law of large numbers” would catch up with AppLovin, and the company could no longer project 20%-30% growth. He also asked Foroughi whether the headroom he promised would come from CTV. Foroughi didn’t think AppLovin would see “accretive” numbers on CTV anytime soon. But there is a pilot program running right now for AppLovin CTV ads.

Shweta Khajuria, of Wolfe Research, put it most directly: “As an ad tech company for investors who are questioning the visibility of your business model and how much confidence you have in the durability of your top-line growth, is there something else incremental that you would consider sharing that would give more confidence in terms of the way your product works?”

For one thing, Foroughi said, AppLovin has delivered strong earnings that exceed investor expectations in 15 of the past 16 quarterly reports. No other large public tech company has its combination of scale, growth rate and profit margin.

Still, the consumer business is too nascent to offer confident predictive benchmarks around its growth or revenue totals, he said. “You sort of have to make your own guesses.”

AppLovin’s earnings can’t just be hand-waved away, nor is its margin vulnerable to any sudden collapse, as happened when Rocket Fuel disclosed a take rate above 60%.

AppLovin is an actual economic force in the mobile economy.

“That ad spend is creating GDP,” Foroughi said. “It’s creating new transactions that otherwise wouldn’t have been there.”

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday heard argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, a case about whether a Texas man on death row can bring a second federal post-conviction challenge to his sentence by arguing that, under updated psychiatric standards, he was found intellectually disabled and therefore cannot be executed.

Except in a few narrow circumstances, the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 bars prisoners from filing a petition for federal post-conviction relief challenging the grounds for their detention when an earlier petition has already been rejected. One of these exceptions is when such a claim relies on “a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable.” The other is if facts “underlying the [initial] claim” would show “by clear and convincing evidence that, but for constitutional error, no reasonable fact finder would have found the applicant guilty of the underlying offense.”

In 2007, Dexter Johnson was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death for his role in the double murder of 23-year-old Maria Aparece and 17-year-old Huy Ngo. Five years before his conviction, the Supreme Court held in Atkins v. Virginia that executing people with intellectual disabilities violates the Eighth Amendment. A defense expert at Johnson’s trial concluded that, under the diagnostic standards employed at the time, Johnson was not intellectually disabled. Following his conviction, Johnson filed an initial habeas petition and invoked Atkins to argue – unsuccessfully – that its protections should extend to people with mental illness.

In May 2013, while Johnson’s first federal petition was pending, the American Psychiatric Association published the DSM-5, a new edition of its diagnostic manual that deemphasized IQ cutoffs. Texas’ highest criminal court adopted this in 2018. In 2019, Johnson scored 70 on an IQ test, and an expert concluded he met the DSM-5’s criteria for intellectual disability. Johnson then filed a successive habeas challenge in the district court claiming that he could not be executed under Atkins. The trial court subsequently ruled that his claim (based on the later diagnostic criteria) had been “previously unavailable,” and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit affirmed that decision. The 5th Circuit denied rehearing, and Texas came to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the case in June.

At oral argument, Texas Solicitor General William Peterson told the justices that Congress “chose to allow new claims in these applications only in limited circumstances that do not include changes in the diagnostic standards for intellectual disability.” There is no “new rule” “previously unavailable” here, because Atkins was decided before Johnson “even committed his crimes,” Peterson said.

Justice Elena Kagan pressed Peterson on why the DSM “isn’t … part of the law?” She suggested that the DSM-5 effectively created “a kind of Atkins I and an Atkins II” – first, a rule barring the execution of people with intellectual disabilities, followed by a “substantive standard” defining what it means to be intellectually disabled. Kagan later described the Atkins standard as akin to a rule with a “big gap in it” where “the DSM comes and plugs it in and it becomes part of the legal standard.”

The justices further debated what it means for a rule to be “available.” Kagan suggested, based on prior precedent, that something is “not available to you” if it makes you “run into a brick wall.” “[I]f I was going to be [previously] laughed out of court,” she said, “then, really, the rule was unavailable to me.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson told Peterson that, as she understood AEDPA, Congress’ “policy choice was to give individuals one clear shot at bringing their constitutional claims.” Under Texas’ interpretation, she said, “Mr. Johnson will never get that opportunity,” which “seems like a really incongruous consequence.”

Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for her part, suggested that the outcome should turn on something like ripeness (whether a case is sufficiently developed for a court to decide). As she remarked to Peterson, “[i]f what we have said under Atkins is you cannot execute someone who is mentally ill, we have a certain way of determining that, and it doesn't become ripe until the DM-5 makes it ripe.”

Justice Brett Kavanaugh asked Peterson whether the court “could resolve this case solely on the new rule issue without addressing ‘previously unavailable.’” Peterson said it could, but that Texas was asking the court to decide the “previously unavailable” question.

On behalf of Johnson, Jeremy Schepers told the justices that “existence and availability aren’t the same thing.” Atkins existed, but Johnson’s claim – based on the change in diagnostic criteria – was not previously available. When the clinical standards for intellectual disability change, Schepers argued, “the Eighth Amendment’s protected class potentially changes as well. And in those rare circumstances, that can render a rule legally available for the first time.”

Justice Clarence Thomas was skeptical, asking, “Does Atkins ever stop being a new rule?” Schepers responded that Atkins “remains new now.” “What about Marbury v. Madison?” Thomas responded. Justice Amy Coney Barrett noted that when “Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone, that was new.” But “I don't think anybody would describe the telephone as new today.”

Kavanaugh pointed Schepers to a “friend of the court” brief filed by Louisiana and 21 other states, which argued that because the medical standards are “constantly evolving,” Johnson’s position is “a recipe for eternal Atkins claims and zero finality.” Schepers said that was incorrect, because a state prisoner gets “one opportunity to raise any claim,” and “so a prisoner could not raise a second Atkins claim.”

At one point, Justice Samuel Alito asked about a future edition of the DSM that “makes smaller changes” that “provide a greater opportunity for success.” Schepers said that claim would fail under the 5th Circuit’s reading, because “[i]t’s only a question of whether the claim had a possibility of merit before.”

Emily Ferguson, an assistant to the U.S. solicitor general who argued as a “friend of the court” in support of Texas, emphasized that it is “difficult to imagine Congress enacting a law that would allow the American Psychiatric Association, without independent action of this Court, to create a new rule of constitutional law.” She also noted that the court had made clear “states would be responsible for the method of determining intellectual disability,” and it would then make little “sense for there to be an available successive application anytime the relevant state had a new … supreme court case … or even a state lower court case that changed the framework that the state was using.”

Alito asked Ferguson whether the “Atkins rule” was “that a person may not be executed if the person has an intellectual disability that is regarded as such by medical professionals,” or if “it is that a person may not be executed if the person has an intellectual disability that can't be justified by the recognized purposes of punishment,” for which “the DSM would be evidence but not part of the standard itself?” Ferguson responded that the “latter formulation captures what … the Atkins Eighth Amendment rule was.”

Perhaps the most noticeable takeaway from oral argument was how subdued the justices were. The chief justice did not ask any questions, and no justice appeared to take up Johnson’s request in his brief that the court dismiss the case as improvidently granted (that is, decide that it was a mistake to have agreed to hear the case in the first place and not resolve it), as the court did last term in Hamm v. Smith, another Atkins case.

A decision is expected by late June but is likely to come earlier.

Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

Zach is the executive editor of SCOTUSblog.

#7554. Agencies Are Not Pitch Perfect; Magnite (And Everyone Else) Bets On Agentic

WPP CEO Cindy Rose recently criticized the rise of “CEO handshake” account wins, which is when an agency skips the pitch but still lands the account through an apparent CEO-to-CEO deal that bypasses the CMO.

“I do not think we do ourselves any favor as an industry of professionals by encouraging clients to bypass proper due diligence,” she told investors last week.

Rose didn’t specifically name Publicis in her references to CEO handshakes, though the holdco’s recent account wins fit the pattern. Publicis landed PepsiCo without pitching, following similar wins for Microsoft in April and LVMH’s APAC account in September.

Publicis, for its part, rejected the characterization in an open letter to Rose, published by Adweek. It begins, “Dear Cindy,” and continues: “Claiming we win on a ‘CEO handshake’ is an insult to clients’ intelligence.”

The letter goes on to note that clients “would never have entrusted us with a task of this magnitude on a wink and a handshake.”

Well, whatever the label, Publicis now owns these accounts and will be accountable if the work falls short.

Happy Daylight Savings and quarterly earnings season.

Magnite, which reported earlier this week, saw a 20% year-over-year revenue increase to $200.6 million in Q3. Connected TV was a highlight (no surprises there), with CTV revenue jumping 39% YOY. CTV has steadily grown as a share of Magnite’s business and now accounts for 53% of the total.

What’s new this quarter, however, is the role of agentic AI. Agentic workflows are infiltrating modern media buying, including for CTV. Agentic media buys can include formats that aren’t yet standardized for programmatic. Think home-screen ads, pause ads and smart TV tiles.

Which is why, during its earnings call, Magnite execs touted how the company is using agentic workflows to sell LG TV home screen inventory.

Magnite is also optimistic about SpringServe, which is not just an ad server, thank you very much. SpringServe is being pitched as a programmatic and mediation platform, a role that helps position Magnite as “the operating system for CTV monetization,” CEO Michael Barrett told investors.

That strategy could pay off as more ad decisioning shifts over to the sell side.

ChatGPT ads are generating less revenue per session than Google Search ads, early data suggests.

Digiday reports that the average is $0.89 for ChatGPT, compared with $2.45 for Google, citing a paper by Maximilian Kaiser and Christian Schulze that is still under review.

One possible reason is limited ad reach. Similarweb and Graphite data show that even in the UK, the market with the highest rate, ads reach just under 46% of eligible ChatGPT users.

And even among users who have seen ads, there’s no set frequency. According to OpenAI, ads appear only when they’re considered additive and relevant to the conversation and never in conversations about sensitive topics.

Yet even with those guardrails, some ads appear to be missing the mark. Paid ChatGPT traffic has a 0.37% conversion rate, compared with 1.17% for Google.

#7552. Supreme Court agrees to weigh in on Goldman Sachs arbitration dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Friday afternoon added a new case to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term, granting a petition for review filed by Goldman Sachs Bank in a case over whether and when a bankruptcy court can override the Federal Arbitration Act and refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes.

The dispute in which the justices agreed to weigh in, Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown, began three years ago, when Rhea Brown and Gregory Maze filed for bankruptcy. Both listed credit card debts with Goldman Sachs Bank as one of their debts.

The Bankruptcy Code imposes an automatic stay, which (among other things) bars creditors from attempting to collect debts from someone who has filed for bankruptcy. Because Goldman Sachs, according to Maze and Brown, repeatedly continued to try to seek payment of their credit card debts, they filed an adversary proceeding (that is, a separate lawsuit within the broader bankruptcy case) against the bank, in which they contended that the bank had willfully violated the automatic stay provision.

Pointing to an arbitration clause in their credit card agreements, Goldman Sachs asked the bankruptcy court to put the adversary proceeding on hold and require Brown and Maze to arbitrate their dispute. The bankruptcy court denied that request, and both the federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld that ruling. A divided three-judge panel of the 4th Circuit concluded that requiring Brown and Maze to arbitrate their claim “would interfere and conflict with the strong and established policies and purposes of the Bankruptcy Code.”

Goldman Sachs came to the Supreme Court in June, asking the justices to take up its case. It told the court that the 4th Circuit’s ruling squarely conflicted with a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit. Moreover, it added, “[t]he practical stakes of these issues are enormous” because of the ubiquity of arbitration clauses in consumer credit agreements. The 4th Circuit’s decision, it said, “imperils the enforceability of arbitration agreements in many of them.”

After considering Goldman Sachs’ petition for review at four consecutive conferences, the justices granted it on Friday afternoon. The case likely will be argued sometime next year, with a decision to follow by late June or early July.

More orders from the justices’ private conference on Friday are expected at 9:30 a.m. EST on Monday.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

The new year will bring a new side job for Justice Clarence Thomas. On Friday, the justices met in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. That afternoon, the Supreme Court announced that, during the conference, the justices added a new case to the oral argument docket: Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown, on whether and when a bankruptcy court can override the Federal Arbitration Act and refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes. For more on the case, see the On Site section below.

Today, the justices will hear arguments in two cases: Nielsen v. Watanabe, on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations; and Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., on whether the “just compensation” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires.

#7547. Reddit tests new search ads

In a blog post published on November 3, Reddit revealed that it’s testing a new ad product. Alongside a “select group of eligible advertisers,” the social platform is experimenting with paid media posts that show up in its search results.

The new ads will harness Reddit’s “existing ad targeting” to surface relevant product recommendations on search pages. The blog post provided two examples of how that process could work: A search for “espresso station” could show results for coffee machines, beans, and mugs, and a query for “home office equipment” could deliver paid listings for monitors, desks, and chairs.

The search ads have plenty of utility for brands that want to reach Reddit’s growing community, which includes a large share of Millennial and Gen Z users. A few years ago, Reddit was cited as the fastest-growing social media site, and its ascendance as a search hub is a big part of that story. As Google stuff its results with AI Overviews, Reddit still delivers answers that are written by humans.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Search ads will turn that competitive advantage into an asset for brands. The new format is part of a broader effort to promote Reddit content while it’s still on Reddit. The platform’s greatest hits often go viral on other platforms, where those posts are sometimes paired with unrelated videos. To keep more traffic in house, Reddit has rolled out a new video product that resembles TikTok.

Paid media in search results promotes Reddit’s homegrown community, but in other areas, the ads will be unable to help Reddit grow its position in the search game. The role of generative AI chatbots in that industry has become a major topic of discussion. Large language models (LLMs) scrape social platforms and use those data points to response to search queries.

Reddit was once the king of chatbot referrals; that advantage inspired other platforms to copy its signature layout. YouTube has since snatched the chatbot referral crown from Reddit.

The LLMs, however, scrape creator content rather than ads. So while Reddit is turning its results pages into an opportunity for brands, those advertisers will still have to link up with creators if they want to meddle with chatbot-based searches.

#7545. Swivel Wants To Create Agentic Infrastructure For CTV

Agentic media buying is the No. 1 topic du jour in ad tech discussion circles. But how does agentic buying even work when it comes to buying TV and streaming ads? Those channels remain more old school and anchored by direct human relationships, at least compared with web display advertising.

TV is a media channel that’s going to have its own particular setup and adoption curve.

At least that’s the thesis behind Swivel, one such agentic ad-buying startup.

Swivel is a publisher tech startup founded by ad tech entrepreneurs and investors: the former FreeWheeler Frans Vermeulen and SpringServe co-founders Matt Dearborn, Rich Lin and Joseph Hirsch. The startup aims to make a name for itself as a company that can automate the manual tasks in publisher ad operations, from campaign optimization to pricing adjustments.

In other words, Swivel wants to be an “end-to-end system” of agents that handles all aspects of campaign management, from media planning to optimization and reporting, Hirsch told Streamlined. The eventual goal, he said, is for an agentic infrastructure that spans the CTV advertising chain in particular and is part of media sellers’ yield optimization.

AI product adoption may seem inevitable. But Hirsch acknowledged that there is no cakewalk in developing agentic solutions for every step in the CTV chain and to gain wide adoption.

Initially, Swivel was “very active in the middle to tail end of the agentic media workflow,” Hirsch said, especially where yield optimization is concerned. But now, he said, “we’re much more active at the front end of the agentic workflow,” referring to campaign functions before any media is purchased, such as planning, forecasting and ad ops rule-setting for guaranteed deals.

Rather than a single consolidated product, Swivel has multiple agents each responsible for parts of a campaign buy, such as budgeting, bid trafficking, pacing, yield management and post-campaign reporting, just to name a few, Hirsch said.

Which is certainly not to say that all publishers are comfortable entrusting their entire media-selling process to AI. Many publishers are interested in using one or two agents, “so as not to disrupt their entire ad ops workflow,” he said. It’s common for clients to pick and choose what they would prefer to outsource to the AI model.

Plus, agentic automation isn’t necessarily simplification. There is a real concern that agentic platforms and MCPs just become another tangle in the fragmentation of CTV media. Plus, with every vendor evolving into an AI solution of some sort, CTV advertisers and ad sellers might easily feel like there are too many agents in the kitchen. (Had to.)

Hirsch said this type of fragmentation is addressed in part by specifications within the Ad Context Protocol (AdCP), a set of standardized protocols for online ad supply chain agents to communicate and negotiate. AdCP includes a specification called adagents.json that allows publishers to declare which agents are authorized to sell their inventory, not unlike sellers.json, Hirsch said. (Editor’s note: The AdCP is collaborative with Prebid and somewhat in opposition to the IAB Tech Lab’s AAMP and ARTF frameworks.)

Agentic media buying on TV screens faces a long, uphill climb, even with optimistic expectations. But there are real perks to incentivize adoption by CTV advertisers and sellers. And those benefits are distinct even from programmatic.

For example, certain non-standard CTV ad formats – such as sponsorship placements, home screen ads and pause ads – can differ across streaming TV apps, smart TV models and CTV buying channels. And without ad standardization across publishers, these CTV buys are difficult to set up programmatically, Hirsch said.

Ad tech vendors and industry orgs have recently announced standardized ways to integrate home screen and pause ads. But it takes time to build wider buy-in.

With agentic media buying, on the other hand, it’s possible to automate ad sales for formats that are unavailable or difficult to buy programmatically, Hirsch said. Along with nontraditional ad formats, he said, sequential media (having creatives appear in a certain order within a program) is another type of buying strategy that can be managed agentically but not programmatically.

Today, “our focus is still 100% CTV,” Hirsch said, but the startup intends to expand into the retail media space, which is especially promising because of the rising overlap between retail media and CTV, he said. Just look at Walmart, Vizio and Vibe.co.

#7543. Netflix might want its new AI search to drum up more “quality” viewership

Netflix‘s new strategy for combating YouTube‘s commanding share of living room TVs is to insist that it’s not the quantity of viewership, but the quality.

And it might be trying to pump up those quality views with a new recommendation tool.

Of course, the times being what they are, the tool is AI.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

AI Discover is intended to curate Netflix’s offerings in a hyperpersonalized manner, so people only see what they like. If this sounds familiar, it’s because Netflix is doing what YouTube, X, and Meta have already done: shunt the responsibility for a quality recommendation algorithm onto viewers and their input.

“There’s more to enjoy and discover on Netflix than ever, but what sounds right for a quiet night in may look different for family movie night or a few spare minutes,” Netflix said in an announcement post. “We’ve spent years refining how you discover, with recommendations tailored to your tastes, from what you Thumbs Up to what you add to ‘My List.’ Now, AI Discover joins the mix as a new way to explore.”

Once a theme is in place, Netflix’s bot brings up a bunch of suggestions, and also additional narrower themes within the first themes. Netflix says there will be a process of “tuning” AI Discover’s recommendations until it “find[s] your next obsession.”

Users who think the bot is getting too far off what they want can refresh the whole deal. Netflix also lets people tell it titles they don’t like.

Unlike the aforementioned social media platforms, Netflix doesn’t seem to have included a ChatGPT-esque discussion aspect to this tool. Users just click through and select what they like, and what they don’t.

Makes sense, since YouTube, Meta, and X have their own in-house chatbots they can shove into everything; Netflix doesn’t have a Gemini or Grok or Muse equivalent, so a yes/no system is its best option. It did partner with OpenAI in 2025 to test an AI search feature that was rumored would replace its regular search function, but that never materialized in full across the service. Maybe this is the version of that idea it ultimately ended up with, sans GPT chatting.

Netflix does say AI Discover is “powered by a new intelligence layer we’ve been building that responds to what members tell us in real time and keeps learning.”

This brings us back to what we said at the top of this article: Netflix is looking for quality viewership. And, well, if it can gather an immense amount of information about viewers’ preferences with this new “intelligence layer,” it might be able to more accurately match them with what they want to watch.

That in turn could drive up the amount of time people spend watching a movie or a TV show–and Netflix might start shooting for average view duration as a way to supercede YouTube.

For now, Netflix’s new AI discovery is only available on TVs in the U.S. (interesting choice), and only in English. Netflix says it won’t appear on kids’ profiles. Per Variety, the streamer plans to expand to more international users in the coming weeks.

#7542. Whose tradition, which history? Agency adjudication and Sun Valley Orchards

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Over the past few decades, several features of the administrative state have been subject to heated constitutional challenge. One of them is agency adjudication: the practice of resolving disputes “in-house” within administrative agencies instead of addressing these disputes directly in a court. Of late, the Supreme Court has applied a “history-and-tradition” methodology to assess the constitutionality of agency adjudication. But that methodology confronts the challenge of how to select from among multiple competing traditions the one that should carry the day. On Nov. 10, the court will hear a case, Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, that underscores the difficulties of carrying out its history-and-tradition methodology – difficulties that apply across many areas of law.

By way of background, the basic constitutional issue regarding administrative adjudication is as follows. Article III of the Constitution vests the “judicial power of the United States” in the Supreme Court and lower federal courts. From the founding and onward, however, disputes that fall within the jurisdiction of Article III courts have been heard in tribunals belonging to the other federal branches, such as territorial courts, military tribunals, bankruptcy courts, magistrate judges, and most pertinent for current purposes, administrative tribunals – for instance, by administrative law judges.

Agency adjudication of, say, Social Security and veterans’ benefits claims is an integral part of the administrative state. It provides a streamlined way of handling these claims and avoids clogging up the Article III courts. Although there is usually a right to appeal administrative determinations at some point to Article III courts, these courts apply a deferential standard of review.

The question arises whether administrative adjudication is compatible with the judicial scheme laid out in Article III of the Constitution. This is a practically significant issue; agency dispute resolution has substantial effects on individuals and companies, who can face considerable fines or penalties. To what extent, then, is agency adjudication outside Article III courts justified? And what kinds of limitations should be placed on it?

In the past few decades, the Supreme Court has turned to “history and tradition” to answer these questions. History and tradition as methods of constitutional interpretation are likely most familiar from cases on hot-button social issues, such as Dobbs (holding that there was no “history and tradition” of a right to have an abortion) and Bruen (holding that there was no “history and tradition” of requiring certain types of licenses to carry firearms outside the home). But the court has also drawn on history and tradition to shape the scope of federal judicial power, in contexts ranging from Article III standing to equitable remedies. One such setting is the division of labor between Article III courts and agency adjudicative bodies.

History and tradition play a dual role in the law of adjudication outside Article III courts. This pattern was on display in the Supreme Court’s 2024 case Securities and Exchange Commission v. Jarkesy, which addressed the constitutionality of agency adjudication of certain claims involving securities fraud. First, tradition provides a justification for non-Article III (including agency) adjudication of a limited class of claims deemed to involve “public rights,” that is, matters which historically “could have been determined exclusively by [the executive and legislative] branches.” In Jarkesy, the court listed “the collection of revenue,” “immigration,” “tariffs,” “relations with Indian tribes,” “the administration of public lands,” and “the granting of public benefits such as payments to veterans, pensions, and patent rights” as members of this class of claims. Since these matters, the court explained, historically could have been adjudicated outside Article III courts, they may be heard by non-Article III tribunals today.

Second, tradition provides a reason that claims involving “private” rather than “public” rights must be brought before Article III courts instead of administrative tribunals. A hallmark of a private-rights suit that belongs before an Article III court, the Jarkesy court stated, is being “made of the stuff of the traditional actions at common law tried by the courts at Westminster in 1789.”

In Jarkesy, the court decided that the securities fraud claim at issue resembled common-law fraud, a traditional common-law claim and so a private right requiring an Article III tribunal. (The court also emphasized that the remedy the SEC was pursuing – civil penalties – was historically enforceable in courts of law; accordingly, the SEC was bringing a suit “at common law” to which the Seventh Amendment jury trial right attached. Jarkesy thus revolved substantially around the jury trial right, which is not a question directly presented in Sun Valley.)

Tradition, then, helps to demarcate the boundary between claims that must be adjudicated by Article III courts (private rights) and claims that may be resolved before other courts, including administrative agencies (public rights). But how should the court decide whether a present-day claim fits into a tradition of private rights or public rights? In particular, what should the court do when there are multiple traditions into which a present-day claim might fit?

The court’s upcoming case Sun Valley provides an example of the problem of “too many traditions.” Sun Valley involves a nonimmigrant visa program, administered jointly by the Department of Labor and the Department of Homeland Security, that permits American employers to hire foreign laborers to perform temporary or seasonal agricultural work. As a condition of participating in the program, employers agree to provide certain workplace arrangements to both foreign and domestic workers. DOL found that Sun Valley, a New Jersey farm, had failed to provide these arrangements, and the agency assessed hundreds of thousands of dollars in civil penalties and back wages against Sun Valley. Sun Valley was required to contest these penalties before an administrative law judge, with deferential review by an Article III court. Sun Valley challenged the administrative-adjudication requirement as a violation of Article III, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit agreed with Sun Valley.

In Supreme Court briefing, the government and Sun Valley both appeal to the history-and-tradition methodology of Jarkesy, but they sharply disagree about which tradition is relevant. The government emphasizes traditions related to immigration. According to the government, its enforcement action fits within two historical categories of public rights adjudication that did not require Article III courts: rights “belonging to the sovereign, such as the right to determine whether to allow aliens into the country,” and “privileges conferred by the government, such as public benefits granted under government programs.” In the government’s view, Sun Valley violated the conditions of bringing foreign workers to the United States through an immigration program that offered the farm a benefit. The pertinent tradition is hence the history of adjudicating immigration- and benefits- related claims outside Article III courts.

Sun Valley, by contrast, casts its claim as akin to common-law breach of contract – a traditional private right requiring an Article III tribunal. DOL’s allegation, Sun Valley observes, was that Sun Valley had violated its agreement to provide certain working conditions to foreign and domestic workers. That allegation, Sun Valley contends, is simply a charge that Sun Valley breached a contract. Sun Valley further argues that DOL sought common-law remedies and in particular civil penalties – more evidence that the claim at issue involves a private right. To Sun Valley, the case is located outside the historical tradition of immigration adjudication because it is based on conditions of employment rather than immigration status. Consequently, it was unconstitutional for DOL to adjudicate Sun Valley’s dispute in-house.

Which party is right about the tradition into which the dispute over Sun Valley’s working conditions falls? Plausibly, the answer is “both.” Yes, the government is alleging that Sun Valley violated an agreement; but the agreement in question was concluded as part of an immigration program allowing Sun Valley to hire foreign workers.

So what are courts to do when, as here, they are faced with “too many traditions” – that is, traditions with different implications for the constitutional question at hand?

One possible response is to conclude that history-and-tradition analysis is hopelessly indeterminate and to reject this methodology. While many methods of constitutional interpretation fail to yield a single right answer, “history and tradition” is often justified precisely by its promise to produce constraint and fixity. Breaking this promise might be viewed as grounds for abandoning the history-and-tradition approach.

Complete repudiation of history and tradition, however, would be unwarranted. Historical practice has played an important role in both upholding and limiting non-Article III adjudication; it is a tool in judges’ toolbox and should not be thrown away.

Another option is to supplement history-and-tradition methodology, when it does not produce a clear result, with other modes of constitutional analysis. Earlier cases on non-Article III adjudication, for instance, appealed openly to practical considerations of government efficiency.

A third option would be to draw on other “modalities” of constitutional interpretation to inform the choice of which strand of tradition to emphasize. One such modality is precedent. Jarkesy did not directly confront a program like the DOL’s in Sun Valley, so it is not controlling precedent. But Jarkesy did seem to treat Congress’ broad power over immigration as a reason to uphold agency adjudication in immigration-related cases. Perhaps this suggests that DOL’s enforcement action fits better into a traditional public-rights than private-rights category.

The court may also decide to avoid the problem of too many traditions by taking a statutory “out.” When it took the case, the court added a question regarding DOL’s statutory authority to impose civil penalties and back wages on Sun Valley. The court may decide that DOL lacks such statutory authority, potentially by appealing to constitutional avoidance (in other words, construing the statute to grant DOL such authority would raise serious questions about the constitutionality of agency adjudication, which should be avoided unless necessary to decide). But the statutory question is not straightforward, and resolving it may well have ramifications for a wide array of agency-imposed penalties. At any rate, one or more of the justices can be expected to opine on Article III in Sun Valley, and the Article III issue is bound to recur.

Overall, the problem of “too many traditions” is by no means unique to the context of non-Article III adjudication. The Supreme Court faces challenging questions about how to apply history-and-tradition methodology when a present-day practice could plausibly fit into multiple traditions. The court’s response to these questions may have an important impact not only on the future of agency adjudication, but also on the trajectory of historically driven interpretation across a variety of pressing constitutional debates.

Rachel Bayefsky is Professor of Law at the University of Virginia School of Law, where she writes about civil procedure, constitutional law, and legal theory. She clerked for Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg in the 2018-2019 Term.

It’s been a hot year for mergers and acquisitions in ad tech and media. But the M&A trend might be due for a cooldown.

Between DoorDash-Instacart, Publicis-LiveRamp, Nielsen-DoubleVerify, Skydance-Paramount and Stagwell-Freestar, there’s been plenty to discuss regarding blockbuster consolidation. And how the political landscape affects such deals is always a prominent talking point.

The thinking goes that Republican administrations – particularly the Trump admin and his DOJ and FTC – are friendlier to mergers between big companies, whereas Democratic administrations apply more antitrust scrutiny.

Plus, regulatory concerns have hung over most of the major acquisitions this year.

The FTC approved Publicis acquiring LiveRamp, but on the condition that Publicis ensures neutrality for LiveRamp’s other customers. Skydance’s Paramount deal was dogged by accusations from Democrats that the companies were bribing President Trump to get the deal approved. And Nielsen faces its own antitrust lawsuit that’s gaining steam.

Meanwhile, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu confirmed that he backed away from a bid to acquire Instacart in 2021 over a perception that the Biden administration would kibosh the deal.

So what are the implications for M&A now that the midterm elections gave Democrats control of the House, the Senate and Congress’s vast investigative power? Will the lame duck portion of the second Trump term be less conducive to consolidation?

The AdExchanger team weighs in on whether this week’s M&A activity – Affle buying Perion for $420 million and Chord acquiring Zenlytic for $5 million – might be the last gasp of a dying trend, or whether there’s still time for more wheeling and dealing.

And, with the midterm elections now behind us, that means sports fans will get a break from the $12 billion onslaught of political advertising. But it also means more room for a $7 billion blitz of gambling and prediction market ads.

AdExchanger’s James Hercher recently penned an opinion column on how the live sports ad experience has felt extra exploitative lately. Call it the enshittification of sports.

His take is that pro leagues and broadcasters are putting marketing dollars above fan enjoyment and even player safety. And he’s got plenty of receipts.

High-end ad blockers mimic some of the same behavior as bot traffic. So WiseGuyGaming repurposed the tools it was already using to identify bots to reveal its ad-blocking audience as well.

Criteo has weathered considerable storms in its day, including a painful moment in March 2020 when its market cap bottomed out below $500 million. Can it pull off yet another turnaround?

Disaffection and outright anger toward US sports institutions run deeper than logo-cluttered fields. Leagues and teams are sacrificing player safety and fan enjoyment for marketing dollars.

#7538. Some students watch thousands of irrelevant videos during class. Can YouTube solve that problem?

Platforms like YouTube have become ubiquitous in classrooms. A recent report from Gallup found that 96% of students are equipped with devices that are meant to enhance their learning.

Reality, however, is not so straightforward. Some students are using their devices to watch videos that don’t qualify as educational. In the most extreme cases, kids and teens watch thousands of those videos each semester; with those behaviors, classroom devices become distractions, not academic aids.

That was one conclusion NBC News drew after surveying student YouTube habits over an entire academic year. The study was not broad — only 11 kids and their parents turned over classroom viewership records — but it was deep. NBC News analyzed more than 17,000 videos and uncovered some concerning trends.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

One Wisconsin sixth grader viewed more than 2,200 videos during the school year, but only 21 were deemed educational. An eighth grader in Pennsylvania watched a whopping 4,700 videos over the same period, and only a small fraction suited the intended use of his classroom device. Those findings echo a recent report published by the Wall Street Journal. That article told the story of a student who watched 13,000 videos on a school-issued device over three months.

To be clear, not all of the students in the NBC News sample are misusing their school devices. Four members of the 11-person cohort mostly used YouTube as intended by viewing educational videos while at school. Around the same time the WSJ report came out, software company Securly tracked classroom traffic and concluded that most students are only on YouTube for about five minutes of the school day.

The educators cited in the NBC News report, however, believe that any kids who are misusing YouTube in the classroom must receive help. “Even if this is just 1% of students, it’s still troubling that this is happening,” BYU Associate Communications Professor Scott Haden Church told NBC News. “It’s something that needs to be understood and regulated.”

As a counterargument, YouTube can claim that it does offer various forms of regulation. Its Player for Education is meant to deliver a distraction-free viewing environment that can keep students from getting off track.

“Our tools allow administrators to block the platform entirely or restrict access to teacher-assigned videos only, with no ads, recommendations, or browsing,” said Google spokesperson Jack Malon in a statement provided to NBC News. “If schools choose to enable browsing for students, we require them to get permission from parents first.”

YouTube itself looks to be taking a different approach. It is working with creators like Mark Rober to develop video-based curricula, and channels like Veritasium have delivered interactive learning experiences to the gaming hub known as Playables.

At this point, YouTube’s presence in classrooms may be inevitable, even if stronger rules are put into place. In that environment, adding positive resources to the platform can help students get the most out of their classroom devices.

#7536. The NYT Opens Pandora’s Letterboxd; Roku Joins The Skulk

The New York Times is in exclusive talks to acquire Letterboxd, the film fan and review site, valuing the publisher at about $330 million. That’s per a recent report from The New York Times, although rumors have swirled all year of a Letterboxd acquisition.

The deal would put Letterboxd’s advertising under the NYT, which should improve its earnings. Letterboxd is reportedly on pace to earn only $15 million this year. It’s not a huge business, but the Times has deliberately pushed into new verticals, often through acquisition: product reviews (Wirecutter), cooking, games (Wordle) and sports (The Athletic).

But one thing that’s often missed in Letterboxd deal discussions – in particular, why it’s sought a high valuation (20x annual earnings) at an absolute nadir for web publisher earnings – is its AI data licensing value.

Letterboxd is an authenticated forum with a massive library of unique human writing that is rich with banter, recommendations, drama, culture, etc. It is, in other words, a rich repository for LLMs.

The New York Times will be more effective at monetizing that asset as well.

Surprise! Fox Corporation announced the completion of its $22 billion Roku acquisition on Friday.

The timing might be unexpected, but the result is not, given that CEO Lachlan Murdoch told investors during last Monday’s earnings call that he expected the deal to close “as soon as possible.” Semafor also reported that the Department of Justice (DOJ) was about to clear the deal under a consent decree, even though it had just recently asked for additional information from both companies in September.

Fox declined to comment to AdExchanger about the deal, but the DOJ’s Antitrust Division released a statement on Friday, saying that the merged company “would suffer monetary and reputational harm if it attempted to use the Roku platform to harm Fox’s content rivals,” and that consumers could easily switch to other connected TV platforms if they were dissatisfied with the product.

Regardless of what happened behind the scenes, Fox now officially owns the top two most popular free streaming services in the US: The Roku Channel (a FAST service) and Tubi (an AVOD streamer). It also has access to all of Roku’s ad tech capabilities and first-party data, allowing the company to massively scale up its connected TV advertising business.

In particular, being able to integrate Roku’s household graph with Tubi’s ad sales would be a real benefit to Fox, which is already seeing more success than it expected from the latter business.

Apple takes the cake with surprise rug-pulling changes. But Google’s no slouch.

For instance, the past few changes have been tough on open web video inventory. CPMs, fill rates and proxies for demand have dropped since about October 26, as Alan Ronis writes at Medium. The Rube Goldberg cascade of events started on October 1, when DV360 removed brand safety controls and thus some advertisers who relied on its finer-grain controls. On October 22, AdSense began restricting more web video inventory based on the accompanying content. And the big whammy was October 26, when Google retired the video line item for mCPV (maximum cost-per-view) campaigns.

The deadline was communicated, but publishers and ad tech didn’t upgrade, and many campaigns that had been preset just failed to serve.

Prebid, by the way, had a similar problem this year because publishers simply couldn’t be made to update their video ad delivery setup when Microsoft reached its deadline for paying to cache all Prebid video ads.

#7532. Publishers: Agentic AI Isn’t About Pricing, But Whether You Get Any Bids At All

The agentic skeptics have the better argument right now.

Anthony Katsur, who runs IAB Tech Lab, expects “several false starts” and years of experimentation and alignment across platforms, agencies and publishers. Razorfish called the mood around agentic AI inevitable – but incremental – at CES back in January.

And Digiday’s research in January found that 54% of 142 brand and agency professionals say their companies don’t use agentic AI in their workflows at all. That is the buy side reporting on itself.

Anyone telling publishers they are already behind on agentic AI is selling something.

However, there’s a fundamental difference between agentic AI and the “inevitable” industry shifts that came before it. Each of those shifts required somebody to build and pay for new integration, and the parties who had to pay disagreed about what to build. The variable is sunk integration cost.

Agentic is the first shift where buyers already paid that bill.

Agentic AI doesn’t face the same barriers. Fully autonomous media buying may still be years away, but AI agents don’t need new pipes or industrywide standards to start evaluating inventory, informing bidding decisions and optimizing spend. They can operate through existing programmatic infrastructure, using integrations the buy side has already built and paid for.

On April 8, 2026, Microsoft ended a relationship with Dentsu that ran for more than a decade and moved its global media planning and buying to Publicis. That mandate carried a price tag the trade press puts between $700 million and $1.2 billion. The media appointment sat inside a larger announcement about embedding agentic AI across the marketing workflow: agents on Microsoft Fabric, informed by Epsilon, deciding which segments matter and deploying media against them.

Asked why Publicis keeps winning without pitches, Arthur Sadoun said clients now understand “it’s about identity.” Publicis also agreed in May 2026 to acquire LiveRamp, a deal the FTC cleared in October subject to a 5-year neutrality order. Once it closes, one of the two largest buyers of publisher inventory will own more of the identity layer that its own agents reason over.

Those agents buy media. Media clears in auctions. Publishers get paid in those auctions.

The industry’s experience with bid shading shows how quickly new buying logic can reshape auctions.

Exchanges began moving to first-price auctions in 2017. Google announced Ad Manager’s move to first-price in March 2019 and finished four months later. Bid shading, a strategy for avoiding paying too much in first-price auctions, spread across SSPs and then DSPs within months via existing integrations, without new infrastructure or industrywide standards.

Publishers, meanwhile, were left to understand bid shading’s impact through their clearing-price reports and adjust their pricing floors accordingly.

Call bid shading machine learning rather than agentic if you prefer. But what’s different this time with agentic is what the logic decides. Shading optimized the price of a bid you were already making. But identity-informed agents decide what inventory is worth a bid at all.

The distinction matters. Publishers risk losing opportunities before their inventory even reaches an auction.

Think of agentic logic as being divided into two halves. IAB research underscores the divide between AI-powered decision-making and autonomous execution. Among 360 digital video buyers surveyed this February and March, 96% see a role for agentic AI in programmatic and RTB, and 63% expect that role to be an optimization layer that improves bidding.

But current adoption, in IAB’s own words, is centered on decision support rather than the purchase decision itself. AI-based deal execution and negotiation for video campaigns sits at 28%. Forty percent of buyers require human approval before an agent acts. That is the shape of it: Agents run freely where no money is committed and get gated where it is.

When Katsur predicts those agentic false starts, he is describing the execution half, and he is right about it.

But the decision-making half is already gaining traction. Among video buyers spending $50 million or more a year, 63% are using or planning to use agents for inventory discovery and evaluation, against 30% of smaller buyers. The largest budgets in the market are pointing agents at deciding which inventory is worth considering.

The exposure is not whether agents will pay a premium for your inventory. It is whether your inventory survives evaluation. Fail that, and you will not be outbid in some future auction. You will not be in the running at all.

Which means the work is the same work it has always been, and it pays now. Publishers don’t need to wait for agentic standards to mature to prepare. Much of the necessary groundwork can also improve performance in today’s auctions.

Here are three steps to take, none of which require knowing which standard wins:

These steps can strengthen inventory evaluation and match rates today, regardless of how quickly autonomous buying develops.

Remember: In 2019, the publishers who understood their own floors before the auction changed did fine. The ones who only learned about the change in buy-side decisioning from their revenue reports did not.

With agentic AI, waiting for fully autonomous transactions could mean missing the more consequential shift already underway.

#7529. TikTok Shop now has a standalone app in four Southeast Asian markets

According to one estimate, the ecommerce market in Southeast Asia will generate $226 billion of gross merchandise value in 2026. TikTok Shop already accounts for a sizable chunk of that GMV, but ByteDance‘s ecommerce hub is looking to increase the size of its market share. With the launch of a standalone Shop app, TikTok will position itself to compete more directly with retailers like Shein and Temu.

Android and iOS versions of the standalone TikTok Shop app have arrived in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and The Philippines. The app was launched with little fanfare, but was spotted by tech consultant Matt Navarra.

With free shipping offers and app-exclusive deals, TikTok is trying to get Southeast Asian consumers to make purchases directly through the new Shop hub. A secure payments platform is also incorporated into the app.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Southeast Asia has long been the backbone of TikTok’s business. By 2022, that region had already delivered more than one trillion TikTok views. With that cultural movement, TikTok usurped traditional streaming services and built the foundation of its ecommerce push.

As TikTok Shop has traveled west, regions like the U.S. have accounted for a greater portion of the platform’s GMV. To capitalize on American spending power, TikTok has announced several partnerships and integrations that will get its Shop ready for the 2026 holiday rush.

It wouldn’t be fair to suggest that TikTok Shop has abandoned its Asian base, but rival platforms have sensed an opportunity to ramp up their activity in Eastern markets. YouTube, for example, has announced a partnership with AliExpress that unites it with one of China’s most prominent retailers.

If the standalone Shop app convinces more consumers to make their purchases directly through TikTok, an international expansion would be a logical next step. That is, however, a big ask — popular ecommerce platforms like Shopee are unlikely to surrender their customers without a fight.
